title: Noah Kahan's Hunger Games Song Is About Grief and Hope
summary:
Noah Kahan has joined the ranks of Taylor Swift and Olivia Rodrigo—by writing a song for a Hunger Games movie. His new track, "Draw You Out," is part of the soundtrack for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping." It may be one of the most memorable songs ever made for the series, which already includes Swift's Grammy-winning "Safe & Sound" and Rodrigo's "Can't Catch Me Now."

The song is emotional and hopeful. In the chorus, Kahan sings: "I carry you on with me / I promised you I would, and I do / And I float around / Show up unannounced in the places that you knew." It's about holding on to someone you've lost.

Kahan is a longtime fan of author Suzanne Collins. Before the song came out, he posted on social media: "This is something I've always wanted to do and I am so grateful for the opportunity to write for this moving film, having adored the works of art by Suzanne Collins." He added that he was inspired by the "tragic yet hopeful story" of Haymitch and Lenore Dove, and that writing about "grief and perseverance through pain" was an experience he'll always be grateful for. He also called the movie "incredible" and said he was honored to be a small part of it.

"Sunrise on the Reaping" is the fifth book in the series and a prequel to the original trilogy. It follows a young Haymitch Abernathy during the 50th Hunger Games. Haymitch was played by Woody Harrelson in the earlier films.

The song reunites Kahan with Aaron Dessner, who co-wrote and co-produced it. They recorded at Dessner's Long Pond Studio in New York, plus Gold Pacific Studios and East Iris Studios in Nashville. The full album, executive produced by Dave Cobb, comes out November 13. The film hits theaters November 20.
why_it_matters: Big franchises use pop stars to pull young audiences toward stories about inequality, violence and grief, so a song like this is not just promotion — it is how a new generation gets introduced to a book series that asks uncomfortable questions about power and who pays the price for it.

background_read: The Hunger Games is a series of novels by Suzanne Collins, an American author who began the story in the 2000s; it is set in a future country called Panem, where teenagers are forced to fight to the death in a televised event called the Games.
The original trilogy — 'The Hunger Games,' 'Catching Fire' and 'Mockingjay' — became four hugely popular films starring Jennifer Lawrence as Katniss Everdeen.

Each film has come with a moody, folk-style song by a major artist; Taylor Swift's 'Safe & Sound' and Olivia Rodrigo's 'Can't Catch Me Now' are the best-known examples, and both were released as part of the official soundtrack.
Aaron Dessner, who worked on 'Draw You Out,' is a member of the band The National and a producer closely associated with Taylor Swift's albums 'folklore' and 'evermore.'
Woody Harrelson is the actor who played the older Haymitch in the earlier films, while this new prequel shows Haymitch as a teenager facing his own Games.

OPEN QUESTION: will the song become as iconic as Swift's and Rodrigo's before it?

perspectives.perspective: Positive — fans of Kahan and the franchise
perspectives.description: Kahan gets a career milestone he says he has always wanted, and the film gains a folk-style anthem that fits the series' habit of pairing dark stories with quiet, sad songs.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — those wary of franchise marketing
perspectives.description: Soundtrack singles are also promotional tools: a popular artist can sell tickets and streams to people who might not care about the film. Some listeners argue that tie-in songs get far more attention than the artist's own albums do.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral — the pattern behind the songs
perspectives.description: The Hunger Games has built a tradition of hiring serious singer-songwriters rather than pure pop acts, going back to Swift's 'Safe & Sound.' That choice keeps the sound of the franchise consistent: acoustic, mournful and aimed at the same teenage audience as the books.

A prequel that follows a young Haymitch could open the door to more films about other tributes and Games, and each one would likely arrive with its own signature song. The album's November 13 release and the film's November 20 opening will show whether the pairing still draws crowds.
